name: Appalachian Log House

revival_periods.note: Recovered twice: first by the Appalachian craft-revival settlement schools and the CCC-era park reconstructions of the 1930s, then by the second-home log industry, which reproduces the silhouette with milled round logs, cathedral ceilings and window walls that the structural system cannot honestly support.

geography.hearth: the Great Valley of Virginia and the southern Blue Ridge

lineage.note: The technique travelled south from the Pennsylvania backcountry down the Great Wagon Road with Scots-Irish and German families between about 1730 and 1780. The notching is German; the plan vocabulary the Scots-Irish applied to it is Anglo.

description.short: The hewn-log single or double pen of the southern mountains: half-dovetail notched oak or chestnut, a stone gable-end chimney, a loft under a steep riven-shingle roof, and an expansion grammar that produced every named Upland South folk house type.
description.long:
The Appalachian log house is the most persistent and best-documented expression of American log building, partly because the technique survived here into the twentieth century and partly because the National Park Service preserved several hundred examples when it emptied the Smokies in the 1930s. The canonical form is a single pen roughly eighteen by twenty feet: walls of eight to ten courses of hewn oak, poplar or chestnut, half-dovetail notched at the corners so every joint sheds water outward, chinked with split-wood spalls and clay or lime, floored in riven puncheon or sawn boards, and covered by a steep roof of hand-split shingles on pole rafters. A stone chimney stands at one gable end, usually outside the wall line, and a loft reached by a corner stair or ladder sleeps the children. One door, one or two very small windows. That is the whole house, and for a great many families in 1830 it was the whole house for a lifetime.

What makes it a design system rather than a hut is the expansion grammar, which is unusually explicit. Because the pen cannot exceed the length of a log two to four people can lift, every increase in size is a combinatorial move on pens: a second pen against the first with a shared chimney (saddlebag); a second pen with its own end chimney and its own front door (double pen); two pens with an open roofed passage between them (dogtrot); a second storey of logs above the first; a rear shed or ell in frame. Henry Glassie's typology of the southern mountain cabin is essentially a grammar of these moves, and it is directly usable as a generative rule set: given a pen and a family, the possible next states are enumerable. This is the property that makes the node valuable to a kit-of-parts system, and it is why the constraint list here is about spans and notches rather than about mouldings.

The conditions are those of settlement in a landscape with abundant hardwood, no roads worth the name, no cash and no sawmills. Scots-Irish and German families moving south from Pennsylvania after 1730 into the Great Valley and then into the coves and hollows of the Blue Ridge and the Cumberlands found a place where timber was the only surplus material and where every alternative building system required something they could not obtain. Log building requires an axe, a broadaxe, a froe, an auger and neighbours. It also produced a house that was warm - a nine-inch solid hardwood wall has enough thermal mass to ride out a mountain night on a banked fire - and that could be built between clearing in spring and frost in autumn. The isolation that made the technique necessary is also what kept it alive for a century after the lowlands had gone to frame, and what made it, by the 1890s, a marker of poverty in the eyes of everybody outside the mountains and a marker of self-sufficiency to everybody inside them.

Standing inside one at Cades Cove or Little Greenbrier, the sensory facts are the wall and the silence. The hewn faces carry the scallop of the broadaxe, and low sun rakes across them so the whole surface reads as a shallow relief. The chinking is a bright band between dark courses and it is the only light-coloured thing in the room. Sound goes nowhere. The single window is small enough that on an overcast day the fire is the light source, and the room organises itself around the hearth in a way that no evenly-lit room ever does. Outside, the eave hangs out two or three feet to keep water off the chinking, the chimney stands proud of the gable in field stone laid without mortar above the firebox, and the roof line is steep because riven shingles will not shed at a low pitch. Nothing about the building is decorative and almost every visible feature is the direct expression of a constraint, which is why it survives being photographed so much better than most American architecture.

defining_characteristics: Single or double pen of hewn hardwood logs, half-dovetail or V-notched at the corners, walls 6-9 inches thick after hewing
Pen dimension 16-20 feet by 14-18 feet, set by log handling limits
Gable-end chimney of field stone, usually standing outside the wall plane, with a stone or clay-and-stick stack
Loft over the single ground-floor room, reached by a boxed corner stair or ladder, lit by a small gable opening
Steep roof (9:12 to 12:12) of riven shakes or shingles on pole rafters or purlins, with deep overhangs protecting the chinking
Very small window openings, cut after the wall was raised, set well clear of the notched corners
Growth by pen combination - saddlebag, double pen, dogtrot, two-storey, rear shed - never by lengthening a log wall
diagnostic_tells: Half-dovetail notching with the log ends sloping outward and downward - the southern mountain signature, distinct from the square notching of the Ozarks and the V-notch of Pennsylvania
Chimney standing entirely outside the gable wall, tapering in field stone
Eave overhang of 24-36 inches on a building with no other refinement whatever
Openings that stop at least two feet short of every corner
Round pole joists with bark intact carrying the loft floor

distinguished_from.difference: The dogtrot is a specific two-pen configuration with an open central passage, and it is common enough in the same region to be modelled separately. A single or contiguous double pen with no open passage belongs here.

Nordic work scribes round or squared logs to a tight chinkless fit, uses steeper roofs and often a full second storey of logs. Appalachian work hews two faces flat and relies on a 1-3 inch chinked gap, which is faster and requires less skill - a deliberate simplification, not a degradation.

The parent node covers the whole continental tradition including Pennsylvania, the Ozarks, Texas and the Old Northwest, whose notching, pitches and plan types differ. This variant is the southern mountain expression specifically.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Entirely material-determined. Log length sets plan dimension, log diameter sets course height, riven-shingle performance sets roof pitch, and the notch sets the corner. There is no applied proportional system and adding one falsifies the type.
typical_ratios: Pen 16-20 feet by 14-18 feet; a near-square plan is normal
Wall 8-10 courses, 7-9 feet to the plate; log course 8-14 inches
Hewn wall thickness 6-9 inches; chinking gap 1-3 inches recessed 1/2-1 inch behind the log face
Roof pitch 9:12 to 12:12; eave overhang 24-36 inches
Door 30-36 inches wide by 5.5-6.5 feet tall; original windows often under 4 square feet
Chimney breast 5-7 feet wide at the base, battering to 2-3 feet at the stack
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: None. Openings are placed by use and by the corner-clearance rule; the apparent front 'symmetry' of a double pen is an artefact of two identical pens, not a compositional decision.

massing_affinities.note: Two equal pens with two front doors and two end chimneys - the standard second stage.
Two-storey log I-houses occur where a family prospered without leaving the technique; they are almost always weatherboarded within a generation.
Where the two pens are deliberately unequal, giving the Anglo social gradient in log.

constraints.statement: No log wall may exceed 20 feet between notched corners; 16-18 feet is normal. Larger enclosures must be built as additional pens. This single rule generates every type in the family and must not be relaxed.

test.note: Tests the hard 20 ft ceiling. The 16-18 ft normal-range and 'built as additional pens' guidance stay prose.

constraints.statement: Corners must be half-dovetail or V-notched with the joint sloping outward to shed water, log ends projecting 2-6 inches beyond the joint. Square-notched corners require pegging and a deeper eave; saddle notching belongs to round-log work and to a different region.

Roof pitch 9:12 to 12:12 with eave and rake overhangs of at least 24 inches. Riven shingles will not shed below 9:12, and the overhang is what keeps water out of the chinking; a clipped eave destroys the wall within a decade.

test.note: Tests the 9:12-12:12 roof-pitch range. Eave/rake overhang (at least 24in) is also cleanly testable via eave_projection_in but is left as prose here since the schema allows one test per constraint.

constraints.statement: Openings must stop at least 24 inches short of any notched corner and must be framed with pegged jambs against cut log ends. Glazed areas larger than about 12 square feet in a single log wall are structurally dishonest to the system.

Chimney at the gable end, outside the wall plane where possible, of laid field stone with a base 5-7 feet wide battering to a 2-3 foot stack. An interior or centred chimney consumes the only room the pen has.

test.note: Tests the gable-end-exterior chimney position ('where possible' softens this to a preference, reflected in the constraint's soft severity rather than in the test). Chimney base/stack width dimensions (5-7ft base, 2-3ft stack) have no vocabulary variable and stay prose.

exemplars.name: John Oliver Place
exemplars.location: Cades Cove, Great Smoky Mountains National Park, Blount County, Tennessee
exemplars.note: Built in the 1820s on the site of an 1818 cabin; the oldest surviving structure on the Cades Cove loop, a single pen with exterior stone chimney and loft.

exemplars.name: Walker Sisters Place
exemplars.location: Little Greenbrier, Great Smoky Mountains National Park, Sevier County, Tennessee
exemplars.note: Hewn logs with half-dovetail notching, stone-and-mud chimneys, and a circa-1838 McFalls cabin dismantled and reassembled as a kitchen wing in the 1870s - the expansion grammar documented in one building. National Register 1976.

exemplars.name: Carter Shields Cabin
exemplars.location: Cades Cove, Great Smoky Mountains National Park, Blount County, Tennessee
exemplars.note: Late nineteenth-century single-pen with a frame addition; useful as evidence that the technique was still current in the mountains sixty years after it had died in the lowlands.

sources: Henry Glassie, 'The Types of the Southern Mountain Cabin', in Jan Brunvand, The Study of American Folklore (1968)
Terry G. Jordan, American Log Buildings: An Old World Heritage (1985)
Michael Ann Williams, Homeplace: The Social Use and Meaning of the Folk Dwelling in Southwestern North Carolina (1991)
National Park Service, List of Classified Structures, Great Smoky Mountains National Park
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2013)

proportion_packs.note: The style's single generative fact -- no log wall exceeds 20 ft between notched corners -- is this pack's own module, and the node's own hard constraint (c01) restates it almost verbatim. Every other proportion in the house is a derived_rule of this one pack keyed to the half-dovetail/V-notch southern-mountain data specifically: pen dimension (log length less notch overhang and wall thickness), wall-log count to the plate, notch overhang and depth by type, gable-end chimney width, dogtrot passage width where present, and porch depth. Bound alone, with no facade, opening or trim pack: the node's own proportional_system says plainly that there is no applied proportional system here and that adding one falsifies the type, and log-module's own window_surround_wood rule states outright that 'there is no architrave, no backband and no casing on the outside of a log wall... applying a moulded surround is the commonest single error in log revival work' -- which makes binding opening-proportion or sash-light actively wrong here rather than merely unnecessary.

declined_packs.reason: The pack dimensions a FRAMED overhang -- `expressed_frame`, `wall_thickness_frame`, a jetty and its drops -- and this node has no frame to jetty. Its corner is a notch and its wall is the structure. The 24-36 in overhang its own record states is an EAVE on a log wall, which is a roof dimension and not a storey oversailing the storey below.
declined_packs.quote: Log length sets plan dimension, log diameter sets course height, riven-shingle performance sets roof pitch, and the notch sets the corner.
declined_packs.note: --impact: governs 0 slots, so this changes no dimension and moves only the meter. Declined rather than left unendorsed because the reading is not close: a framed overhang on a notched log pen is a category error, and leaving it unjudged invites the next pass to spend the reading again.

The pack does not merely fail to fit; the record forbids the category.

declined_packs.reason: A second-to-first-storey ratio needs a stack of storeys to graduate. This node's canonical form is a single pen with a loft over it, and its own wall figure is stated once, per storey, in log courses -- there is no piano nobile to be taller than an attic. Same reading as the four single-storey declines of 28 Aug.
declined_packs.quote: The canonical form is a single pen roughly eighteen by twenty feet
declined_packs.note: --impact: governs 1 slot, `stair_type`, which loses ALL dimensioning on the decline -- stated rather than hidden. A log loft is reached by a ladder or a boxed corner stair, and a figure derived from a graduated Georgian stack was never the right one for it; no dimension is better than a wrong dimension, which is this corpus's own rule. It also ARMS `structure.graduation_check`, so endorsing was the alternative and would have made every plan of this style answerable to a ratio its record refuses.

declined_packs.reason: The pack's whole claim is that in a brick building every horizontal dimension is a whole number of COURSES off the mason's rod. This node states the same idea with a different module: the course is a log, and its depth is the log's diameter. Two coursing systems cannot both dimension one wall, and the record names which one this is.
declined_packs.note: --impact: governs `steps_and_stoop`, which on the decline passes to `palladio-tuscan` (italian-renaissance) rather than losing dimensioning. Worth stating plainly: declining a wrong pack can hand the slot to a pack that is wronger, and OQ 58's limit -- a decline stops a pack, it does not supply one -- is doing real work here. The successor is itself an unendorsed delivery and is in the ruling table.

declined_packs.reason: A 16-20 ft structural bay measured off English and Anglo-American BOX FRAMES, with partitions and jambs falling near the posts. This node's pen is 16-20 ft for the opposite reason -- a log is as long as it is -- and there are no posts for anything to fall near. The figure coincides; the mechanism it comes from does not exist here.
declined_packs.note: --impact: governs `eave_condition`, which passes to `facade-picturesque`; nothing loses dimensioning. THE COINCIDENCE IS THE POINT and is why this was read rather than pattern-matched: a pack whose headline number matches the node's own is the easiest wrong endorsement to make.

declined_packs.reason: It dimensions `wall_thickness_frame` and `expressed_frame` -- a framed wall with panel infill. This node's wall is solid hewn log and its own record carries the thickness, so the pack is not filling a gap; it is overwriting a stated measurement with one derived from a construction the building does not use.
declined_packs.note: --impact: governs 3 slots; `primary_cladding` and `wall_thickness_frame` lose all dimensioning and `expressed_frame` passes to `facade-medieval-english`. The two losses are the honest outcome: a log wall has no cladding layer and no frame to thicken, and the record's own 6-9 in is the number a reader should be sent to. `wall_thickness_masonry`/`_frame` are among the four slots no fault covers, so nothing was checking this figure either.

declined_packs.reason: The pack's assembly is a masonry-coped gable -- kneeler, coping run, apex stone -- and its parapet rule is guarded on a parapeted or shaped gable_treatment. This node's gable is the end of a shingled roof on pole rafters above a log wall. There is no coping, no parapet and no screen.
declined_packs.quote: covered by a steep roof of hand-split shingles on pole rafters
declined_packs.note: --impact: governs `cornice_return`, which loses all dimensioning. That is right rather than regrettable: a cornice return is a classical eave detail and this node's own record says the eave is a 24-36 in overhang 'on a building with no other refinement whatever'. The pack was supplying a figure for a member the building does not have. NOTE this is the SAME pack whose 13 Craftsman-family deliveries are the ruling table's largest single question -- there the gable is present and the pack's TREATMENT of it is what is in doubt; here the treatment and the member are both absent, which is why this one is decidable from the record and those are not.

This is a further instance of oq/a-node-that-refuses-a-category-must-decline-it-twenty-six-times: with this one the node has refused twelve packs, of which FOUR are order-systems (chambers-doric, palladio-corinthian, palladio-doric and this) and the other eight are module, trim and facade systems. An earlier draft said 'the same category twelve times', which counts twelve declines of five different kinds as one category; the adversarial check that caught it proposed five orders, which is also wrong. The figure here is measured from each pack's own `kind`.
